title: US Measles Cases Hit 35-Year High as School Vaccination Rates Slide Below Safety Threshold
excerpt: With over 2,300 confirmed cases in 2026 — surpassing last year's record before August — public health officials warn the country may lose its measles elimination status as kindergarten MMR coverage drops to 92.5 percent.
body:
• The US has recorded over 2,300 measles cases in 2026, surpassing the entire 2025 total and reaching the highest count since 1991.
  • Kindergarten MMR vaccination coverage has fallen from 95.2% to 92.5% nationally — below the 95% herd immunity threshold — with states like Idaho, Utah, and Oregon reporting far steeper drops.
  • Epidemiologists at Johns Hopkins say the US will likely lose its measles elimination status, a designation it has held since 2000.
  • Indian-American families face compounded risk from declining US school vaccination rates and exposure during summer travel to South Asia, where measles remains endemic.

The United States has blown past its 2025 measles record with five months still left in the year. The CDC reported 2,318 confirmed cases as of July 24, according to data updated Friday, while Johns Hopkins University's tracker had logged 2,295 cases earlier in the week. Either figure eclipses the 2,289 total for all of 2025 — itself a 33-year high at the time.

The last time annual US measles numbers were this elevated was 1991, when 9,643 cases were reported during a multi-year resurgence that prompted the introduction of a second MMR vaccine dose for children.

"I would be shocked if we don't lose our elimination status."

— William Moss, epidemiologist, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health

Why Cases Keep Climbing

The surge traces directly to eroding vaccination coverage. Nationwide, MMR uptake among US kindergartners dropped from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.5% in 2024–2025, according to CDC data — well below the 95% threshold epidemiologists say is necessary to prevent sustained community spread.

In some states, the gap is far more alarming. Oregon's kindergarten nonmedical exemption rate climbed to a record 10.9% for the 2025–2026 school year, with only 85.6% of kindergartners up to date on required vaccines. Utah sits at 88.6% MMR coverage. Idaho's nonmedical exemption rate has reached roughly 15.4%, meaning about one in seven kindergartners enters school without full immunization documentation.

"In communities with pockets of susceptible individuals across a broad age range, measles has been able to take hold, infecting those who are susceptible and spreading rapidly," Moss said in a Johns Hopkins release.

Two explosive outbreaks drove much of this year's count. South Carolina's Spartanburg County outbreak — the largest single measles cluster since elimination was declared in 2000 — reached 997 cases before being contained in April, costing the state $2.1 million. Utah's outbreak continues to simmer. Cases have now been reported in more than 40 states, plus Washington, D.C., and New York City.

Elimination Status at Risk

The US achieved measles elimination status in 2000, meaning the virus was no longer continuously transmitted within the country. That designation now hangs by a thread. If endemic transmission is confirmed for 12 consecutive months, the status will be revoked — as it was for Canada in November 2025, which triggered the loss of elimination status for the entire WHO Region of the Americas.

"This has been long in the making," Moss told Science News. He pointed to the wide age distribution of cases — roughly 20% in children under five, 50% in 5-to-19-year-olds, and 30% in adults over 20 — as evidence that under-vaccination has accumulated over many years, not just during the recent pandemic-era dip.

"Successful vaccination programs undermine themselves because people forget how devastating these vaccine-preventable diseases can be," he said. "Much of the public has forgotten the deaths and disability due to smallpox, polio, measles."

A Familiar Challenge for the Diaspora

For Indian-American families, the US outbreak carries echoes of a long-running battle at home. India's second-dose measles vaccine coverage stood at just 31.9% among children aged 24 to 35 months in the most recent National Family Health Survey, far short of the 95% target set for measles elimination by 2026. Bangladesh, across the border, is grappling with close to 50,000 confirmed cases and over 800 deaths this year alone.

The WHO reported progress in 2024 — India cut its number of zero-dose children by 43%, from 1.6 million to 900,000 — but coverage across South Asia remains below the 95% threshold. For diaspora families traveling to the subcontinent this summer, health officials recommend verifying MMR status before departure. The virus circulates widely in parts of Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Kerala, and Gujarat.

Within the US, the CDC's SchoolVaxView tool allows parents to check vaccination coverage at the state and district level, revealing pockets of vulnerability that statewide averages can mask. With the fall school year approaching, pediatricians are urging parents to bring children's immunizations up to date.

What Comes Next

Public health expert Jessica Steier called the crisis "a problem of our own making and completely preventable."

"Measles will continue to find susceptible communities next year and beyond. That means more outbreaks, more quarantines, more school and childcare disruptions."

— Syra Madad, epidemiologist

Steier stressed that the problem remains "recoverable" — the US eliminated measles once and can do it again by restoring high MMR coverage and responding rapidly to every case. But Moss warned that the withdrawal of US funding from global health organizations, including the WHO and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, threatens immunization programs worldwide, compounding the domestic crisis with a global one.

For now, the message from every corner of epidemiology is blunt: check your vaccination records, check your children's school's rates, and get the shot before fall.
